card: In India it is a defined meteorological event, and the definition is not simply "very hot".
answer: In India a heatwave is a formally defined event, declared by the India Meteorological Department when the maximum temperature at a station clears a zone-dependent floor and departs far enough from that station's own normal. It is a departure from local normal, not an absolute temperature — which is why 41°C can be a heatwave in one city and an ordinary May day in another.
explainLead: A single national temperature threshold would declare a heatwave in Rajasthan every summer and never declare one in Shillong.
explain: Heat harms people relative to what they are adapted to. A population, a housing stock and a working day built around 45°C summers is not in the same danger at 44°C as a hill town at 32°C. IMD's criteria are built on that: a station has to be hot in absolute terms and unusually hot for itself.

So there are two gates. First a floor by zone — the plains, the coast and the hills each have their own. Then a departure from that station's own normal maximum for the date, or, separately, an absolute temperature high enough to qualify on its own regardless of departure.

IMD declares for a subdivision, not for a point, and requires the criteria to be met at two or more stations. A single hot grid point is not a declared heatwave — it is a day meeting the criteria at a location.

defs.d: The long-period average maximum temperature for that station on that date. The reference every departure is measured from.
How far above normal the day's maximum ran, in °C. The core of the criteria.
IMD's meteorological unit for declarations. Larger than a city, smaller than a state in most cases.

standard.head: IMD's thresholds
standard.lead: Two ways to qualify. Either the departure route or the absolute route.
after: There is no legal limit here. Nobody can break a heatwave criterion — it is a definition, not a standard, and this is one of the places on this site where the reading is measured against a threshold that regulates nothing.

readHead: How to read a heat figure
readLead: Almost every misreading of Indian heat data comes from one of three confusions.
measure: Declared or qualifying? IMD declares for a subdivision on two or more stations. A dataset that counts days meeting the temperature criteria at single grid points — including this site's — is counting a related but different thing, and should say so.

Maximum or apparent temperature? The criteria use dry-bulb maximum. What a body experiences depends on humidity too, and a coastal 38°C at high humidity can be more dangerous than an inland 44°C. The criteria do not capture that.
Station-days or heatwave days? Summing qualifying days across fourteen stations gives station-days, which is not a national count of heatwave days.
cannot: It cannot tell you about night-time heat, which is the better predictor of mortality. A hot night gives a body no chance to recover.
It cannot account for humidity, and therefore cannot describe the coastal danger that dry-bulb temperature misses.
It cannot be compared internationally. Every meteorological agency defines a heatwave differently, and most define it relative to their own climatology.
It says nothing about exposure — who is outdoors, in what work, in what housing. That is what turns a temperature into a death.
